headline: AI as tutor and as measurer: colposcopy training for residents, and heart MRI ejection fraction compared with clinicians
intro: One review covers a randomised trial in which an AI virtual-patient platform improved OB/GYN residents' diagnostic reasoning but not their operative skill. The other covers a large Lancet Digital Health study where AI ejection-fraction measurements from cardiac MRI predicted death slightly better than expert clinicians' measurements, which raises the question of what trainees still need to learn to do by hand.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-enhanced colposcopy training improves diagnostic reasoning and communication competencies: A randomized controlled study
items.source: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.summary: In a randomised, assessor-blinded, wait-list trial, 60 PGY-2 and PGY-3 obstetrics and gynecology residents at two affiliated teaching hospitals added an AI virtual-patient platform to their usual colposcopy teaching either straight away or a month later. At one month the AI group scored higher on case analysis (78.57 vs 71.03, a mean difference of 7.54), diagnostic justification and communication, but operative competence did not differ (p = 0.113), and both groups were proficient by three months. It was a small, single-specialty trial with short follow-up, scored on OSCEs rather than patient care.
items.why_it_matters: AI virtual patients look like a way to speed up practice in diagnostic reasoning and communication. Programs should not assume that talking a case through with an AI builds hands-on procedural skill.

items.title: Performance of artificial intelligence versus clinician left-ventricular segmentation of cardiac MRI for mortality prediction: a retrospective, multicentre, prognostic study
items.summary: The task was outlining the left ventricle on cardiac MRI to measure ejection fraction and other volume measures, and then using those measures to predict death from any cause. A deep-learning segmentation tool was compared with expert clinicians' segmentation of the same scans from 27,382 patients at UK and US centres who had known or suspected heart disease. Over an average follow-up of more than five years there were 3,458 deaths. In Cox models, AI-derived ejection fraction predicted mortality 'marginally' better than clinician-derived ejection fraction. The difference was statistically significant and held after adjusting for factors such as age and sex. The AI took about 2–3 seconds per patient, against roughly 13 minutes for expert analysis in the team's earlier work, and it made errors in about 1% of patients. The main limitations: the study was retrospective, it measured how well each set of numbers predicted death rather than any effect on care or outcomes, the gain was small, and the senior author invented the AI tool.
items.why_it_matters: Ejection fraction decides who gets heart-failure drugs, devices and procedures. If AI measures it at least as well as experts, trainees' time may be better spent checking and interpreting the numbers than producing them. The roughly 1% error rate is a reminder that someone still has to know what a wrong contour looks like.
